content: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer and the fourth leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women worldwide, with an estimated 570,000 new cases and 311,000 deaths reported in 2018. It is more prevalent in younger women, particularly those aged 25 to 45 years. A woman’s lifetime risk of developing cervical cancer by the age of 65 varies significantly, ranging from 0.8% in high-income countries to 1.5% in low-income countries. Over 85% of cervical cancer deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries, highlighting significant disparities in prevention and treatment access. The geographical variation in cervical cancer incidence and survival rates is closely linked to the availability of primary and secondary prevention strategies, as well as the prevalence of high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) infections. Persistent infection with hrHPV is the primary cause of nearly all cervical cancer cases. To date, over 100 types of HPV have been identified, with 14 classified as high-risk types. HPV types 16 and 18 are associated with approximately 75% of cervical cancers and precancers globally, except in Asia, where the association is slightly lower. In Western and Central Asia, 82% of invasive cervical cancers are linked to HPV 16/18, compared to 68% in Eastern Asia. Early cervical cancer is often asymptomatic. When symptoms do occur, abnormal vaginal bleeding, particularly post-coital bleeding, is the most common presentation. Advanced disease may present with dyspareunia, pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, and non-specific symptoms such as changes in urinary or bowel habits and weight loss. Detection of cervical abnormalities during screening or in symptomatic cases often leads to colposcopy and biopsy for histological diagnosis. Cervical cancer management strategies vary globally and depend on the disease's grade and stage, as well as national healthcare resources and policies. Survival rates decrease with increasing age. In Europe and the USA, the five-year survival rate ranges from 63% to 72%, while in Taiwan, Korea, and Japan, it is between 70% and 77.3%. Prevention strategies focus on reducing known risk factors (primary prevention) and early detection and treatment of pre-invasive disease (secondary prevention). Persistent hrHPV infection is the most critical risk factor for cervical cancer, with studies estimating a worldwide HPV prevalence of 99.7% in cervical cancers. Other risk factors include smoking, early age at first sexual intercourse, multiple sexual partners, the presence of other sexually transmitted diseases, and compromised immune status. Individuals receiving immunosuppressive therapy for organ transplants or those infected with HIV are at higher risk of developing pre-invasive disease. Primary prevention strategies aim to reduce these risk factors through vaccination, smoking cessation, and promoting safer sexual behaviors. Prophylactic HPV immunization before exposure to the virus is the most effective intervention for primary prevention. HPV vaccines are made from viral capsid proteins that self-assemble into virus-like particles (VLPs), which are non-infectious as they lack viral DNA. Four HPV vaccines have been developed: monovalent (HPV 16), bivalent (HPV 16 and 18), quadrivalent (HPV 16, 18, 6, and 11), and nonavalent (HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58). All except the monovalent vaccine are licensed for use. The vaccines stimulate an immune response by producing antibodies against hrHPV. Their cancer-preventive effect lies in preventing persistent hrHPV infections that lead to high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and adenocarcinoma-in-situ (AIS), precancerous conditions that can progress to cervical cancer. Three-dose schedules of the monovalent, bivalent, and quadrivalent vaccines have shown effectiveness against precancerous conditions and persistent hrHPV infections in females aged 15 to 26 years, with no increase in serious adverse events. After five to eight years of vaccination, the prevalence of HPV 16 and 18 decreased by 83% in girls aged 13 to 19 years and by 66% in women aged 20 to 24 years, providing compelling evidence of the vaccines' effectiveness. A study published in 2020 demonstrated a significant reduction in cervical cancer incidence in populations with high HPV vaccine uptake, particularly among those vaccinated as younger adolescents. Two-dose regimens of the bivalent, quadrivalent, and nonavalent vaccines provide equivalent immunity compared to three-dose regimens, with stronger antibody responses when the interval between doses is six to 12 months. The quadrivalent vaccine offers similar protection to the nonavalent vaccine in reducing the incidence of high-grade CIN, AIS, and cervical cancer in individuals aged nine to 26 years. It also decreases the incidence of external genital lesions among boys aged 10 to 26 years. Many countries have implemented HPV immunization programs. In the UK, HPV vaccination is part of the routine schedule for boys and girls aged nine to 13 years. Vaccines protect against hrHPV infection in individuals naive to the virus but are ineffective in those with pre-existing HPV infections, who remain at risk of developing cervical cancer. Therefore, secondary prevention methods, such as screening for hrHPV nucleic acids and abnormal or precancerous cell changes, remain essential for reducing cervical cancer risks. Cervical screening aims to detect and treat precancerous changes early. More than 90% of cellular abnormalities occur in a small area of the cervix called the transformation zone. Because the disease progresses slowly, there is time to detect and treat precancerous lesions before they become invasive cancer. Conventional cervical screening involves the Papanicolaou (Pap smear) test, targeting women aged 25 to 65 years. During screening, a healthcare professional uses a speculum to visualize the cervix and collect cells from the transformation zone, which are then examined in the laboratory for cytological changes. Guidelines for screening frequency vary by country, but most recommend screening every one to five years. The quality of the Pap smear test depends on accurate specimen sampling and preparation. Up to 10% of Pap smear test results are classified as inadequate, leading to repeated smears and increased burden on the healthcare system and women. Liquid-based cytology (LBC) was developed to improve the diagnostic reliability of the Pap smear test. Unlike conventional smears, LBC involves transferring the cervical sample into a vial containing a fixative solution, where blood and other obscuring material can be separated. Studies have found LBC to be a reliable and cost-effective technique with superior sensitivity and lower rates of inadequate samples compared to Pap smears. In high-income settings, national cervical screening programs have successfully reduced cervical cancer incidence and mortality. However, there is a marked disparity between high-income and lowand middle-income countries regarding access to standard screening tests and funding for national screening programs. While more than 80% of high-income countries have cervical cancer policies and strategies, cervical cytology is generally available in only 35% of countries in the African Region. Consequently, 85% of cervical cancer cases and deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries. Socioeconomic status, ethnic origin, age, and education affect screening uptake. Studies have found lower uptake rates in older women, those less well-educated, from lower socioeconomic groups, and residing in rural locations. Certain ethnic groups, including African-American, Hispanic, and Native American women in the USA and Asian women in the UK, report lower rates of cervical screening uptake. Interventions to encourage screening uptake must consider these sociodemographic factors and available resources. Conventional screening is undergoing a conceptual change with the introduction of primary hrHPV testing as a method of secondary cervical cancer prevention. This involves testing the screening sample for the presence or absence of hrHPV. If hrHPV is not detected, the woman is offered routine screening again in three to five years, depending on her age. If hrHPV is detected, cytological analysis is performed to assess for precancerous changes, and colposcopy is offered if required. Self-sampling for hrHPV testing is an alternative to clinician-collected samples. Women can use a swab or soft brush to collect a vaginal sample, which is analyzed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based or signal amplification (SA)-based assays. PCR-based assays are superior to SA-based assays in sensitivity for detecting high-grade lesions. Self-sampling is highly acceptable to women and could improve screening uptake, particularly in lowand middle-income countries where trained cytopathologists and suitable infrastructure are limited. Offering hrHPV self-sampling may lead to higher screening participation rates compared to reminder invitations for cytology. Mailing self-sampling kits appears to provide higher population coverage than opt-in strategies. However, primary HPV testing cannot distinguish between transient and clinically significant hrHPV infections, necessitating triage assessment for cervical lesions. Current recommended triage involves cytology, which is less effective on self-collected samples. Alternative triage strategies, such as repeated self-sampling and molecular methods, require further validation. Cervical cancer incidence decreases with increasing screening frequency. Extending the re-screening interval from every year to every three years results in a minimal excess risk. In the UK, women aged 25 to 50 years are invited for screening every three years, and those aged 50 to 64 years are invited every five years. Despite its effectiveness, the uptake rate of cervical screening by eligible women is only 75% in the UK. Globally, 65% of countries have introduced national cervical screening programs, but only 12% have achieved an uptake above 70%. Research has shown that primary screening for hrHPV followed by cytology triage of HPV-positive women is more effective than cytology-based screening. In 2016, the UK National Screening Committee recommended adopting hrHPV testing as the primary strategy, and as of December 2019, primary hrHPV screening has been fully implemented across England. Further research is needed to establish whether hrHPV self-sampling could be an effective strategy to increase screening uptake rates.
